name: North-South Choke from Kesa Gatame
description: Complete guide to the North-South Choke from Kesa Gatame in BJJ. Detailed execution steps, defensive counters, safety protocols, and training progressions.
overview:
The North-South Choke from Kesa Gatame leverages the existing head control and arm trap of scarf hold to set up one of the most reliable blood chokes in grappling. Unlike entering the North-South Choke from standard side control, the Kesa Gatame entry provides a pre-established choking arm position around the opponent's head, reducing setup time and minimizing defensive windows. The attacker uses the perpendicular angle of Kesa Gatame to thread the choking arm deep before rotating toward the opponent's head, creating a seamless transition that catches many defenders off-guard.

The mechanics rely on chest-to-face shoulder pressure combined with the arm encircling the neck to compress both carotid arteries simultaneously. The attacker's sprawling weight drives the choking shoulder into one side of the neck while the wrapped arm compresses the opposite carotid. From Kesa Gatame, the natural rotation toward the opponent's head places the choking arm at ideal depth, which is the primary advantage over other entries. The finish requires patience and precise hip positioning rather than explosive squeezing, as the choke tightens progressively with proper sprawl pressure.

Strategically, this technique functions as a high-percentage chain from Kesa Gatame when the opponent defends Americana and Kimura attempts by keeping their arms tight. The transition to the choke punishes the defensive posture that defeats arm attacks, creating a forcing function that makes the entire Kesa Gatame position significantly more dangerous at all belt levels.

injury_risks.injury: Carotid artery compression leading to loss of consciousness
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate recovery if released promptly; potential for longer-term effects if held after unconsciousness

injury_risks.injury: Tracheal compression and windpipe damage from misaligned pressure
Neck strain from bridging attempts during defense
Cervical spine stress from improper release or continued pressure after tap
injury_risks.recovery_time: Weeks to months depending on severity

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum to allow partner to recognize the danger and tap
tap_signals: Multiple rapid hand taps on opponent's body
Multiple rapid foot taps on the mat
Any distress signal including body convulsions
Loss of resistance or going limp
release_protocol: Immediately release arm pressure and remove shoulder compression upon any tap signal
Roll off opponent's head and neck area completely
Allow opponent to recover in side-lying position with airway clear
Monitor for signs of consciousness and normal breathing
Never move opponent's neck immediately after release - allow them to move naturally first
training_restrictions: Never apply explosive or jerking pressure to the neck during the rotation or finish
Always ensure partner has clear tap access with at least one hand
Never hold the choke after partner taps or goes limp
Beginners should practice the transition and grip placement only, without applying actual choking pressure
Use progressive resistance drilling before live application

variations_and_setups.description: The fundamental entry where the attacker threads the choking arm deep from standard Kesa Gatame head control, then rotates the body toward the opponent's head while maintaining arm depth. The rotation is smooth and continuous, with chest pressure maintained throughout the transition.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When you have established solid Kesa Gatame control and the opponent is relatively flat and defending arm attacks

variations_and_setups.description: The attacker threatens an Americana on the trapped near arm, forcing the opponent to defend by tucking their elbow tight. This defensive reaction opens the neck and allows the attacker to thread the choking arm deeper before initiating the rotation to North-South. The Americana attempt serves purely as a setup for the choke.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the opponent is actively defending arm attacks by keeping elbows tight to their body

variations_and_setups.description: Starting from Modified Scarf Hold where the underhook replaces the head wrap, the attacker switches the underhook to a head wrap while sliding toward the opponent's head. This entry works when the attacker is already controlling with Modified Scarf Hold and recognizes the choke opportunity.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When transitioning from Modified Scarf Hold where the underhook position provides initial access to thread around the neck

attacker.name: from Kesa Gatame Attacker
attacker.description: How to execute the North-South Choke from Kesa Gatame. Step-by-step finishing mechanics, grip details, rotation timing, and counter responses.
attacker.overview: Attacking the North-South Choke from Kesa Gatame requires mastering a smooth rotational transition that maintains choking arm depth throughout the movement. The key advantage is that your head-controlling arm from Kesa Gatame becomes the primary choking mechanism, eliminating the separate grip-fighting phase that standard North-South Choke entries demand. Success depends on threading the arm deep before initiating rotation, controlling the near arm to prevent defensive frames, and finishing with heavy sprawl pressure rather than muscular arm squeezing. The transition is most effective when chained after failed Americana or Kimura attempts, as the opponent's tight-elbow defensive posture creates the ideal opening for deeper arm threading and smooth rotation toward the head.
key_principles: Thread the choking arm to maximum depth under the opponent's neck before initiating any rotation toward North-South
Maintain continuous chest-to-face pressure throughout the entire transition to prevent the opponent from creating frames or turning
Control or pin the opponent's near arm before rotating to eliminate the primary frame that blocks the transition
Use sprawling hip pressure to generate choking force rather than squeezing with the arms, which fatigues quickly and reduces effectiveness
Time the rotation when the opponent is defending arm attacks, as their tight-elbow posture opens the neck for deeper arm threading
Keep your body tight against the opponent during rotation with no space between your chest and their head at any point
setup_requirements: Established Kesa Gatame with your arm wrapped securely around the opponent's head and neck, with the forearm reaching toward their far-side carotid
Opponent's near arm trapped under your armpit or pinned against their body so they cannot create frames during rotation
Opponent flat on their back with shoulders on the mat and no effective frames against your upper body pressure
Your choking arm threaded deep enough under the opponent's neck that your forearm contacts or passes the centerline of their throat
Stable base with your hips low and far leg posted wide, allowing you to initiate rotation without losing positional control

execution_steps.description: Establish tight Kesa Gatame with your arm wrapped deep around the opponent's head. Your forearm should be threaded under their neck with your hand reaching past the centerline of their throat toward the far-side carotid artery. Squeeze their head against your ribs and keep your hips heavy.
execution_steps.timing: Hold for 5-10 seconds to settle weight and confirm control

execution_steps.action: Thread Choking Arm to Maximum Depth
execution_steps.description: Use small incremental movements to walk your choking arm deeper under the opponent's neck. Each time they exhale or adjust, slide your forearm another centimeter deeper. Your goal is to get your bicep pressing against one side of their neck while your forearm and wrist wrap around to compress the other side.

Pin the opponent's trapped near arm against their body using your elbow pressure or by clamping it between your arm and torso. This arm is the primary tool they will use to frame against your shoulder during rotation. If it is free, they can post and prevent the transition entirely.
execution_steps.timing: 2-3 seconds to confirm arm is controlled

execution_steps.description: Begin pivoting your body toward the opponent's head by stepping your far leg over and walking your hips in an arc. Maintain chest-to-face contact throughout the rotation. Your choking arm stays locked in position as your body rotates around it. Do not lift your chest off their face at any point during the pivot.

execution_steps.action: Arrive in North-South and Secure Finishing Grip
execution_steps.description: Complete the rotation so your chest is directly on the opponent's face and your hips are sprawled behind you. Connect your hands using a gable grip or grab your own bicep with the free hand. Your choking arm should now be wrapped fully around their neck with your shoulder driving into one carotid and your forearm compressing the other.
execution_steps.timing: 2-3 seconds to settle and lock grip

execution_steps.action: Sprawl and Drive Shoulder Pressure to Finish
execution_steps.description: Drive your hips toward the mat and forward into the opponent while squeezing your elbows together. Your shoulder drops heavy into the side of their neck while the encircling arm tightens the opposite side. The choke tightens as you sprawl and walk your hips slightly toward their far shoulder. Maintain steady progressive pressure until they tap.

execution_steps.action: Fine-Tune Angle if Choke Is Not Finishing
execution_steps.description: If the opponent is surviving the initial pressure, micro-adjust your angle by walking your hips slightly toward their choking-arm side. This changes the compression vector on the carotid arteries. You can also try pulling your choking elbow tighter toward your own hip to increase arm compression while maintaining sprawl pressure with your hips and chest.

common_counters.counter: Framing against the shoulder during rotation to block the transition to North-South
common_counters.your_response: Pin their near arm before rotating. If they frame with the far arm, use your free hand to strip the grip and pin it against their chest before completing the rotation.

common_counters.counter: Turning into the attacker and recovering closed guard during the rotation
common_counters.your_response: Maintain heavy chest pressure and sprawl your hips to prevent them from turning their hips toward you. If they partially turn, redirect to mount transition instead of forcing the choke.

common_counters.counter: Bridging explosively to create space and disrupt the arm threading phase
common_counters.your_response: Ride the bridge by posting your far leg wide and keeping your hips low. Use the moment after the bridge when they return to the mat to thread deeper, as post-bridge is when they are most flat and exhausted.

common_counters.counter: Tucking chin and turning head away to block arm from reaching deep enough
common_counters.your_response: Use your free hand to cross-face and turn their chin back toward you, or apply pressure with your chest to their jaw to create the angle needed for deeper arm threading. The chin tuck delays but rarely prevents a committed attacker.

common_errors.error: Rotating before threading the choking arm to sufficient depth under the neck
common_errors.consequence: The arm slides out during rotation and you arrive in North-South without a choke, wasting the transition and allowing the opponent to escape or recover guard
common_errors.correction: Spend additional time in Kesa Gatame walking the arm deeper with small incremental movements before initiating any rotation. The arm should reach past the centerline of the throat before you begin to pivot.

common_errors.error: Lifting chest off the opponent's face during the rotation to North-South
common_errors.consequence: Creates space that allows the opponent to frame, turn, or insert their arms between your chest and their face, blocking the choke completion entirely
common_errors.correction: Maintain continuous chest-to-face contact throughout the rotation. Think of your chest as glued to their face, with your body pivoting around that contact point. Walk your legs in an arc rather than lifting and repositioning.

common_errors.error: Squeezing primarily with arm strength rather than using sprawl pressure to finish
common_errors.consequence: Arms fatigue rapidly within 10-15 seconds, the choke loosens as you tire, and the opponent survives long enough to mount an escape
common_errors.correction: Generate choking force through your hips and shoulders by sprawling hard and walking your hips forward. Your arms maintain the grip position while your body weight and sprawl do the actual compressing. This is sustainable for minutes rather than seconds.

common_errors.error: Failing to control the opponent's near arm before initiating rotation
common_errors.consequence: Opponent posts their near arm against your shoulder and physically blocks the rotation, stalling the transition and forcing you back to static Kesa Gatame
common_errors.correction: Before rotating, pin their near arm by clamping it between your elbow and torso or pressing it flat against their body with your hip. Confirm the arm is controlled before taking the first rotational step.

common_errors.error: Rushing through the rotation instead of maintaining steady pressure throughout
common_errors.consequence: Gaps open between your body and the opponent during fast movement, giving them frames and escape opportunities they would not have against slow controlled pressure
common_errors.correction: Move deliberately and slowly through the rotation, treating each degree of pivot as its own micro-position that must be consolidated. The entire rotation should take 3-5 seconds, not a sudden explosive spin.

common_errors.error: Arriving in North-South with hips too high off the mat
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient downward pressure on the neck means the choke lacks compression force, and the opponent can slide out from under you or turn to escape
common_errors.correction: As you complete the rotation, immediately sprawl your hips flat toward the mat. Your belt line should be close to the ground. Walk your toes forward to drive additional downward pressure through your shoulder into their neck.

training_progressions.focus: Arm threading depth and Kesa Gatame control
training_progressions.description: Practice threading the choking arm to maximum depth from Kesa Gatame without rotating. Partner lies still while you work on incremental arm walking, weight distribution, and finding the correct forearm-to-carotid alignment. Drill 20 repetitions per side focusing on depth alone.

training_progressions.focus: Smooth transition from Kesa Gatame to North-South without losing arm depth
training_progressions.description: With the choking arm pre-set at depth, practice the rotational pivot from Kesa Gatame to North-South. Partner provides zero resistance. Focus on maintaining chest-to-face contact throughout the rotation and arriving in North-South with proper sprawl position. Drill 15 repetitions per side.

training_progressions.focus: Sprawl pressure, grip connection, and angle adjustments for the tap
training_progressions.description: From the completed North-South position with arm threaded, practice connecting the finishing grip and applying progressive sprawl pressure. Partner taps when they feel the choke engage. Work on the micro-adjustments of hip angle and shoulder drive that make the difference between a choke that finishes and one that stalls.

training_progressions.focus: Combining Americana threat into choke entry under progressive resistance
training_progressions.description: Start from Kesa Gatame and threaten the Americana. When partner defends by tucking their elbow, use the opening to thread the choking arm deep and execute the full rotation and finish. Partner increases resistance each round. Practice reading the defensive reaction that signals it is time to transition to the choke.

training_progressions.focus: Full-speed positional sparring starting from Kesa Gatame
training_progressions.description: Positional rounds starting from Kesa Gatame with the top player hunting the North-South Choke among other submissions. Bottom player defends at full resistance. Focus on timing the transition correctly during live exchanges and recognizing when the choke is available versus when to stay in Kesa Gatame and continue with arm attacks.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the North-South Choke from Kesa Gatame primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The choke targets both carotid arteries simultaneously. The shoulder drives into one carotid while the encircling arm compresses the opposite carotid. When both arteries are occluded, blood flow to the brain is cut off, causing unconsciousness within seconds. The trachea may also experience secondary compression, but the primary mechanism is bilateral carotid compression making this a blood choke rather than an air choke.

flashcards.question: Why must the choking arm be threaded to maximum depth before initiating the rotation from Kesa Gatame?
flashcards.answer: If the arm is not deep enough before rotation begins, the rotational movement causes the arm to slide out from under the opponent's neck as your body pivots. You arrive in North-South without sufficient arm depth to compress the far-side carotid, and the choke will not finish regardless of how much sprawl pressure you apply. Re-threading from North-South is much harder than getting depth from Kesa Gatame where head control is already established.

flashcards.question: Your opponent defends the Americana by pinching their elbow tight to their ribs - how does this create an opening for the North-South Choke?
flashcards.answer: When the opponent tucks their elbow to defend the Americana, they pull their arm away from blocking your choking arm's path under their neck. Their defensive posture also tends to flatten them onto their back with minimal framing, which is the ideal position for threading the choking arm deeper. The tight-elbow defense that stops the Americana is exactly the posture that enables the choke, creating a true dilemma where defending one attack opens the other.

flashcards.question: What is the correct way to generate finishing pressure - arm squeezing or sprawling?
flashcards.answer: Finishing pressure must come primarily from sprawling your hips toward the mat and walking them forward, driving your shoulder weight into the opponent's neck. The arms maintain grip position but do not generate the primary compression force. Arm squeezing alone fatigues within 10-15 seconds and produces inconsistent pressure, while sprawl-based pressure uses your entire bodyweight and can be sustained for minutes. The shoulders squeeze together as a consequence of the sprawl, not from active arm contraction.

flashcards.question: What are the key safety considerations when applying the North-South Choke in training?
flashcards.answer: Apply pressure slowly and progressively over 3-5 seconds minimum, never explosively. Always ensure your partner has at least one hand free to tap. Watch for any distress signals including body going limp, convulsions, or loss of resistance, as the choke can render someone unconscious very quickly once both carotids are compressed. Release immediately upon any tap signal and roll completely off the opponent's head and neck. Never continue applying pressure after a tap to demonstrate the position.

flashcards.question: How should you release the North-South Choke immediately after your partner taps?
flashcards.answer: Immediately release all arm pressure and remove your shoulder from their neck. Roll your body completely off their head and neck area rather than simply loosening the grip while remaining on top. Allow your partner to recover in a side-lying position with their airway completely clear. Monitor them for normal breathing and signs of full consciousness. Never manipulate their neck after release - let them move naturally. If they appear unconscious, place them in recovery position and alert the instructor immediately.

flashcards.question: The choke feels close but your opponent is surviving your sprawl pressure - what micro-adjustment should you try?
flashcards.answer: Walk your hips slightly toward the choking-arm side to change the compression angle on the carotid arteries. This small lateral shift often closes the gap between almost-finishing and a clean tap. You can also try pulling your choking elbow tighter toward your own hip to increase the arm's compression while maintaining sprawl weight. Another adjustment is driving your shoulder forward and slightly downward, aiming to press the bony point of your shoulder directly into the carotid groove on the neck.

defender.name: from Kesa Gatame Defender
defender.description: How to defend and escape the North-South Choke from Kesa Gatame. Recognition cues, early-stage prevention, escape timing, and guard recovery techniques.
defender.overview:
Defending the North-South Choke from Kesa Gatame requires early recognition of the rotational transition and immediate frame creation to prevent the attacker from settling into the choking position. The critical defensive window occurs during the rotation itself, when the attacker is transitioning between positions and is most vulnerable to guard recovery or re-establishing frames. Once the choke is fully locked with sprawl pressure applied, escape becomes extremely difficult, making prevention and early intervention the primary defensive strategy rather than late-stage escape attempts.

The defender must prioritize keeping their chin tucked to limit arm threading depth, maintaining frame contact with the attacker's shoulder to block rotation, and being ready to turn into the attacker to recover guard before the rotation completes. Understanding the attacker's sequencing allows the defender to identify which phase the attack is in and apply the appropriate counter at each stage.
key_principles: Recognize the arm threading phase early - deeper arm depth means less chance of successful defense once rotation begins
Frame against the attacker's rotating shoulder before they complete the pivot to North-South, as this is the highest-percentage defensive window
Keep your chin tucked toward your chest to reduce the space available for the choking arm to thread under your neck
Turn your body toward the attacker during the rotation rather than away, as turning toward them enables guard recovery while turning away exposes your neck further
Maintain at least one arm free for framing at all times - if both arms become trapped the choke becomes nearly inescapable
Act early and decisively rather than waiting to see if the choke will fully lock, because late defense against this choke has very low success rates
recognition_cues: The attacker begins incrementally walking their arm deeper under your neck from Kesa Gatame, making small adjustments rather than maintaining static head control
The attacker pins or controls your near arm more tightly than normal Kesa Gatame requires, suggesting they are preparing to rotate
The attacker's body begins pivoting or their far leg starts stepping over in an arc toward your head side
You feel increasing forearm pressure across the front of your throat as the choking arm reaches deeper past the centerline
The attacker threatens an Americana then quickly abandons it when you defend, immediately redirecting to thread their arm deeper around your neck

defensive_options.action: Frame against the attacker's shoulder with your far arm to block the rotational transition before they reach North-South
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you feel the attacker beginning to pivot their body toward your head, before they complete the rotation
defensive_options.if_successful: Attacker is forced to abandon the choke attempt and returns to standard Kesa Gatame control where you can work standard escapes
defensive_options.risk: If the frame is weak or placed too late, the attacker can swim past it and complete the rotation with the choke partially set

defensive_options.action: Turn your hips toward the attacker and work to recover closed guard by getting your knees between your bodies during the rotation
defensive_options.when_to_use: During the mid-rotation phase when the attacker is between Kesa Gatame and North-South and their base is least stable
defensive_options.if_successful: You recover closed guard and the choke attempt is fully neutralized with you in a relatively safe position
defensive_options.risk: If the attacker's arm is already deep enough, turning toward them can actually tighten the choke as you rotate into the compression

defensive_options.action: Grip fight to prevent the choking arm from threading deep enough by using your near hand to push against their forearm or wrist under your neck
defensive_options.when_to_use: During the early threading phase while still in Kesa Gatame, before any rotation has started
defensive_options.if_successful: The attacker cannot achieve sufficient arm depth and the choke will not finish even if they complete the rotation to North-South
defensive_options.risk: Grip fighting with your near arm may allow the attacker to isolate it for an Americana or Kimura if you extend too far

defensive_options.action: Bridge explosively and turn onto your side away from the attacker to create space and potentially scramble to turtle
defensive_options.when_to_use: As a last resort when the rotation is nearly complete but the choke grip is not yet fully locked
defensive_options.if_successful: You create enough space to prevent the choke from locking and may recover a defensive position
defensive_options.risk: If the arm is deep, bridging away can tighten the choke rather than relieve it, and you expend significant energy

escape_paths: Frame against the attacker's shoulder during early rotation, push their upper body away, and hip escape back to re-establish Kesa Gatame bottom position where standard escape sequences apply
Turn your hips toward the attacker during mid-rotation, insert your knees between your bodies, and work to close your guard around their torso before the choke locks
Grip fight the choking arm from underneath to prevent sufficient depth, then use the stalled attack to create space for a bridge-and-turn escape back to turtle or half guard

favorable_outcomes.how: Turn your body toward the attacker during the rotation phase, get your hips underneath them, and close your legs around their torso to recover full closed guard before the choke can lock in North-South
Frame against the attacker's shoulder to block the rotation completely, forcing them to abandon the choke and return to standard Kesa Gatame where you can resume normal escape sequences

common_errors.error: Waiting until the attacker has fully arrived in North-South before beginning any defensive action
common_errors.consequence: Once the attacker is settled in North-South with the choking arm locked and hips sprawled, escape success drops below 10 percent and the choke finishes rapidly
common_errors.correction: Defend during the threading and rotation phases while the attacker is between positions. Your defensive window is during the transition, not after it completes.

common_errors.error: Pushing the attacker away with extended arms rather than turning your body toward them
common_errors.consequence: Extended arms create space but do not address the choking arm position, and straight-arm pushing from your back generates minimal force while exhausting your shoulders
common_errors.correction: Turn your entire body toward the attacker to recover guard rather than trying to push them off from a supine position. Turning creates structural defense while pushing is just muscular resistance.

common_errors.error: Turning your head away from the attacker when you feel neck pressure, exposing the far-side carotid
common_errors.consequence: Turning your head away opens the neck and allows the choking arm to sink deeper, actually accelerating the choke rather than defending it
common_errors.correction: Keep your chin tucked firmly toward your chest and turned slightly toward the attacker. This compresses the space under your neck and makes arm threading more difficult.

common_errors.error: Ignoring the arm threading in Kesa Gatame because you do not recognize the choke setup
common_errors.consequence: The attacker achieves maximum arm depth unopposed, making the subsequent rotation and finish nearly guaranteed
common_errors.correction: Learn to recognize incremental arm walking under your neck as a direct threat. Any time the attacker adjusts their head-controlling arm deeper in Kesa Gatame, immediately begin defensive grip fighting on that arm.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that the North-South Choke from Kesa Gatame is being set up?
flashcards.answer: The primary cues are the attacker incrementally walking their arm deeper under your neck with small adjustments, increased control or pinning of your near arm, and the attacker's body beginning to pivot toward your head. You may also feel increasing forearm pressure across the front of your throat as the choking arm threads past the centerline. If the attacker threatens an Americana then quickly abandons it to adjust their head-controlling arm, this is a strong signal the choke is being set up.

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to tap when caught in the North-South Choke?
flashcards.answer: Tap rapidly and clearly with whichever hand is free, either on the attacker's body or audibly on the mat. If both hands are trapped, use rapid foot taps on the mat or give a clear verbal submission. Do not wait to see if you can survive the choke, because this particular choke can cause unconsciousness within 3-5 seconds once both carotids are compressed. Tap early when you feel the pressure building rather than waiting until you feel lightheaded, as the margin between controlled pressure and unconsciousness is very small.

flashcards.question: Why is defending during the rotation more effective than defending after the attacker reaches North-South?
flashcards.answer: During the rotation, the attacker is between positions with compromised base and divided attention between maintaining arm depth and completing the pivot. Their weight is shifting and they cannot simultaneously apply maximum choking pressure while moving. Once they arrive in North-South and sprawl their hips, they have full bodyweight driving the choke with stable base, and all their attention is on finishing. The transition phase is where the attacker is weakest and your frames and guard recovery attempts have the highest success rate.

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available against the North-South Choke from Kesa Gatame?
flashcards.answer: The three primary defenses are: first, framing against the attacker's shoulder during early rotation to physically block the pivot and force them back to Kesa Gatame; second, turning your hips toward the attacker during mid-rotation to recover closed guard before the choke locks; and third, grip fighting the choking arm from underneath during the threading phase to prevent sufficient depth. The appropriate defense depends on which phase the attack is in, with earlier intervention yielding higher success rates.

flashcards.question: What common mistake makes the choke tighter when attempting to defend?
flashcards.answer: Turning your head away from the attacker is the most counterproductive defensive reaction. When you turn your head away, you expose the far-side carotid artery and create more space under your neck for the choking arm to sink deeper. This instinctive response actually accelerates the choke rather than defending it. Instead, keep your chin tucked firmly toward your chest and turned slightly toward the attacker to compress the available space under your neck and make arm threading more difficult.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying the setup cues and understanding the attack timeline
training_progressions.description: Partner slowly walks through the North-South Choke setup from Kesa Gatame at 25 percent speed while you practice identifying each phase: arm threading, near arm control, rotation initiation, and North-South arrival. Call out each phase verbally as it happens. Repeat 15-20 times to build automatic pattern recognition.

training_progressions.focus: Developing the shoulder frame that blocks the rotation
training_progressions.description: Partner initiates the rotation at 50 percent speed. Practice placing your frame against their shoulder at the correct timing and angle to prevent rotation. Focus on structural alignment of the frame rather than muscular pushing. Drill 20 repetitions per side with partner providing feedback on frame placement and timing.

training_progressions.focus: Turning into the attacker and closing guard during the rotation window
training_progressions.description: Partner rotates at 75 percent speed and moderate resistance. Practice the full defensive sequence: recognize rotation, frame to slow it, turn hips toward attacker, insert knees, and close guard. Gradually increase partner resistance over multiple rounds. Success is defined as recovering any form of guard before the choke locks.

training_progressions.focus: Full-resistance defense starting from Kesa Gatame with attacker hunting the choke
training_progressions.description: Positional rounds starting from Kesa Gatame with the top player using the North-South Choke among other attacks at full resistance. Defender works all available defenses and escapes. Two-minute rounds with roles switching. Track success rate and identify which defensive phase needs the most work.
